a.note: A softer "and/but" that links a contrast or turns the question back: "Dobro sam, a ti?"

aerodromu.note: Locative of aerodrom; "na aerodromu" = at the airport

ajde.note: Short form of hajde. Used to nudge, encourage or agree

ajte.note: Plural or polite form of ajde

anu.note: Ana in the accusative: "pitaj Anu" = ask Ana

badnje.note: In "Badnje veče" = Christmas Eve, Orthodox, January 6

banci.en: in the bank; at the bank

baš.note: Adds emphasis: baš lepo = really nice

bela.note: "Bela kafa" = white coffee; matches the noun

belo.note: Neuter form, matches a neuter noun

bi.note: Helper word for "would" (conditional): on bi došao = he would come

bih.note: "I would": ja bih. Also used in ne bih rekao = I wouldn't say so

bila.note: Past tense of biti for a woman or a feminine noun

bili.note: Past tense of biti for a group

bilo.note: Past tense of biti for "it"; also "bilo šta" = anything

bio.note: Past tense of biti for a man

bolja.note: Matches a woman or feminine noun

bolji.note: Matches a man or masculine noun

brate.note: Calling a man "brat" (vocative). Used for friends, not just family

bre.note: Filler word for emphasis, to a friend. Casual, can sound rough to elders

briga.note: "Baš me briga" = I couldn't care less

crkoh.note: Slang for "I'm dying": past tense, I (male or female)

da.note: Yes, but also joins phrases: hoću da idem = I want to go

do.note: "Do viđenja" = until we see each other

do đavola.note: Same as do vraga, more old-fashioned

dobar.note: Matches a masculine noun: dobar dan

dobar dan.note: The polite daytime hello, for elders and strangers

dobra.note: Matches a feminine noun: dobra ideja

dobro.note: The all-purpose "good". Doesn't change when used as an adverb

dobro veče.note: After about 6 PM. Polite or casual

dopadaš.note: "Dopadaš mi se" = I like you (a bit like sviđaš)

doviđenja.note: Short for "do viđenja", a polite goodbye

dođem.note: "Ne mogu da dođem" = I can't come

dođite.note: Command for a group or a person you're polite to

draga.note: To a woman you care about (pet name) or "dear" in a letter

drago.note: "Drago mi je" = nice to meet you

drago mi je.en: nice to meet you; I'm glad

dvoje.note: For a couple or mixed group: "nas dvoje" = the two of us

engleski.note: The language name. Not capitalized in Serbian

evo.en: here; here it is; here I am

fali.note: "Fali mi" = I'm missing it / I miss it

ga.note: Short form of "him" as an object: pitaj ga = ask him

gdje.note: Ijekavian form (Bosnia, Croatia, Montenegro). In Serbia you'll say "gde"

gostoprimstvu.note: From gostoprimstvo; Serbs take this very seriously

haljinu.note: "Volim tvoju haljinu" = I love your dress

hristos.note: In the Christmas greeting "Hristos se rodi!"

hristos se rodi.note: Orthodox Christmas greeting. Reply: "Vaistinu se rodi"

ima.note: "Ima li…?" = is there…? "Šta ima?" = what's up?

imam.note: "Imam" for I have; negative is nemam

inat.note: A Serbian trait: refusing to bend, even when it hurts you

izađemo.note: "Hoćeš da izađemo?" = want to go out?

izvolite.note: Offering to elders, strangers, or a group

je.note: From biti. Weak word: sits after the first stressed word

jebote.note: Vulgar exclamation, literally "f*** you". Used for shock

jesam.note: Emphatic "I am" in a yes answer

kafa.note: Serbian coffee is strong, served with a glass of water

kao.note: Also "as if" or "kind of": kao da = as if

košta.note: "Koliko košta?" = how much does it cost?

l'.note: Spoken short form: "Je l' si gladna?" = "Jesi li gladna?"

laku noć.note: Literally "light night". Say it before bed

lep.note: Said to a man. Feminine: lepa

lepa.note: Matches a woman or feminine noun

lepo.note: Doesn't change as an adverb. Ijekavian: lijepo

li.note: Turns a statement into a yes/no question: "Jesi li gladna?"

ljubavi.note: Calling her/him "my love" (vocative). Also: of love

ljutiš.note: "Zašto se ljutiš?" = why are you mad?

ludilo.note: Used as a reaction: "Ludilo!" = crazy! / wow!

ma daj.note: "Ma" adds attitude to "daj" (give). Disbelief or encouragement

majka.note: Formal/proper for "mom": mama is used day to day

majke.note: In "majke mi" = I swear (on my mom)

mala.note: Also a sweet "my little one" for a girl

malo.note: "Malo" is used as a softener everywhere

mene.note: Stressed form of me: "mene" (after a preposition or for emphasis)

meni.note: "Meni je dobro" = it's good for me

mi.note: Two jobs: "we" (mi smo) and short "to me" (sviđaš mi se)

milo.note: "Milo mi je" = I'm glad; also "milo" = sweet

miru.note: "Daj mi mira" = leave me in peace

mislim.note: "Mislim da…" = I think that…. "Mislim na tebe" = I'm thinking of you

mog.note: Genitive/accusative of moj: "ljubav mog života" = love of my life

molim te.note: "Te" = you. Use with friends and family

molim vas.note: "Vas" = you (polite / plural). With elders and strangers

momak.note: Used for a guy / a boyfriend

mora.note: "Mora da je kasno" = it must be late

na.note: "Na" is the all-purpose preposition: on, at, to, onto

najbolji.note: Superlative of dobar: "najbolji prijatelj" = best friend

nas.note: "Nas je troje" = there are three of us

nazdravlje.note: Toast: to your health. Also what you say after a sneeze

nađemo.note: "Gde da se nađemo?" = where shall we meet?

ne.note: Goes right before the verb: ne znam

nedostaješ.note: "Nedostaješ mi" = I miss you. Fališ mi is more casual

nezgodan.note: Careful: it doesn't mean "inconvenient" only; also awkward

nikad.note: "Nikad" before ne: nikad ne znam = I never know

odavno.en: for a long time; long ago

ovaj.note: Also used as a filler, like "um"

pa.note: Filler that links a thought: "Pa, ne znam…" = well, I don't know…

pita.note: Savory pastry like burek-style pie. Also "he/she asks"

planinu.note: "Idemo na planinu" = we're going to the mountains

po.note: "Doći po tebe" = to come pick you up

polako.note: A way of life: don't rush

politici.note: "O politici" = about politics. Often a touchy subject

pozdravi.note: "Pozdravi mamu" = say hi to your mom

pozivu.note: "Hvala na pozivu" = thanks for the invitation

prelepa.note: Stronger than lepa: "prelepa si" = you're stunning

prijatno.note: What you say before a meal: bon appétit

pun.note: "Pun sam" = I'm full / "kafić je pun" = the cafe is full

rakija.note: Fruit brandy. A must at Serbian gatherings; often homemade

roditelje.note: "Pozdravi roditelje" = say hi to your parents

sastanak.note: Could mean a work meeting or a date

se.note: Part of reflexive verbs: "zovem se" = I'm called

sit.note: "Sit sam" = I'm full (man). Woman says "sita sam"

slava.note: A family's patron saint day. Big feast, open house

slobodna.note: "Kad si slobodna?" = when are you free?

smaraj.note: Slang: "ne smaraj me" = don't bug me

smeha.note: "Umirem od smeha" = I'm dying of laughter

super.note: Works as an adjective or a one-word reply: "Super!"

sve najbolje.note: Used for birthdays and as a general warm wish

sviđam.note: "Sviđam ti se?" = do you like me?

te.note: Short "you": "volim te" = I love you. Also "those" (plural)

ti.note: Casual "you" to one friend; also short "to you" in some sentences

tip.note: "On je super tip" = he's a great guy

troje.note: "Nas je troje" = there are three of us

tucamo.note: At Easter: "tucamo jaja" = we tap-crack eggs

umirem.note: "Umirem od smeha" = I'm dying of laughter

uskrs.note: Orthodox Easter, a different date from Western Easter

vaistinu.note: Old-fashioned Easter reply: "Vaistinu vaskrse!" = truly He is risen

vi.note: Use with elders, strangers, or several people

video.note: Past tense, man: "video sam" = I saw. Also "video"

videćemo.note: "Videćemo se" = see you / we'll see each other

volim.note: "Volim te" = I love you. Also "I like (it)"

vuk.note: "Gladan kao vuk" = hungry as a wolf

za.note: "Za tebe" = for you; "za sat" = in an hour

zafrkavaš.note: Slang: "zafrkavaš me" = you're messing with me

zovem.note: "Zovem se Met" = my name is Matt

ćevapi.note: Small grilled minced-meat sausages; a national dish

žao mi je.note: Literally "pity to me is". Sympathy or a light apology

žuri.note: "Žuri mi se" = I'm in a hurry

žurku.note: "Idemo na žurku" = we're going to a party
